messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Matthias Brandt is a 37-year-old German-American financial analyst who was referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating occupational impairment and a recent separation from his therapist of two years, who had retired. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 59, consistent with severe posttraumatic stress. The precipitating trauma occurred approximately three years ago when Matthias was taken captive during a business trip abroad. He was held for eleven days in a series of confined spaces — a van, a basement room, and finally a concrete cell — by individuals whose demands were never made entirely clear to him. The conditions were degrading: he was kept in near-total silence for long stretches, occasionally broken by the distant sound of children crying somewhere in the structure above him. His captors handled him with an impersonal physical efficiency — moving him, restraining him, positioning him — that stripped him of any sense of being a person in their eyes. He was eventually released without explanation. No one was ever charged.

In the years since, Matthias has found that the world has become reorganised around a set of sensory thresholds he cannot control. The sound of children crying — something he now encounters regularly in the open-plan office building where he works, as a daycare operates on the floor below — pulls him immediately back into that basement. When the crying filters up through the ventilation system during the afternoon hours, his body floods with alertness, his attention fractures from his spreadsheets, and he finds himself scanning the room for exits. That same hypervigilance floods in when he encounters sudden, complete silence — the kind that falls when a conference call drops or when the office empties unexpectedly at the end of the day. Both sounds, and the absence of sound, function as direct activations of his threat system: within seconds of either, he is superalert, scanning, unable to locate safety even inside familiar spaces. He has difficulty falling asleep most nights not because he fears nightmares specifically, but because some part of him remains convinced that lowering his guard is dangerous — that the moment he stops listening, something will happen.

When threat is already elevated, his memories become harder to hold at a distance. Matthias describes his recollections of the captivity as possessing an almost hallucinatory quality — more vivid and present than anything from his ordinary life, as though the event is still happening in some layer of his nervous system. He can sometimes smell the damp concrete and the particular chemical odour of the restraints, and these sensory intrusions feel less like remembering than like being returned. The heightened state of arousal that accompanies his vigilance seems to lower the threshold for these intrusions, so that an afternoon of scanning and listening in the office can give way, by evening, to hours in which the memories press close and vivid against the present.

What the memories return him to, again and again, is not only the fear but the moral injury. Matthias has come to believe that he behaved in ways that contradict who he understood himself to be — complying, acquiescing, doing what was required of him to survive — and this belief sits in him like a verdict. He feels, at times, like something that was used rather than a person who endured something. The knowledge that the men responsible have faced no legal consequences compounds this: justice has not reorganised the world, and so the wrongness of what happened remains, in his view, unresolved and somehow still ongoing. These appraisals feed back into his sensitivity to the world in specific ways — physical affection, a colleague's hand on his shoulder, his daughter's hug during custody visits, reactivates the memory of being handled without consent, and the shame and dehumanisation surface immediately, making warmth feel like a threat.

Matthias sought help again after missing three consecutive custody visits — not because he did not want to see his daughter, but because the daycare adjacent to his ex-wife's apartment building meant that children's voices were unavoidable on arrival. He is most afraid, he says, that he will never be able to tolerate closeness again. What he is hoping for, more cautiously, is to stop feeling like the captivity is still in progress.
